Wildfires expose unexploded bombs across Europe THE WILDFIRES BURNING across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from the World Wars that threaten crews responding to the flames. Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944. Fuelled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant. “Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions and also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them. This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group. In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the south-western city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be Second World War era ammunition. In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, governor Herve Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. Advertisement He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb. The wreckage of a Second World War German warship emerges in front of Djerdap II, a large dam on the Danube River. The fire, which stretches across the border into Germany, is smouldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around this area. The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops. Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany. Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons. In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. This also exposed the hulls of dozens of Second World War German battleships In the middle of the river separating Serbia and Romania near the Serbian port of Prahovo, a rusty hull is now visible along with a broken mast where the Nazi flag used to fly. People look at the wreckage of a Second World War German warship in front of Djerdap II, a large dam on the Danube River, between Romania and Serbia, near Prahovo, Serbia (Darko Vojinovic/AP) Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from the Second World War emerged at its base in receding water. The US, Russia and China are working on space weapons, which could include signal jammers to disable satellites. Photograph: Ronan Lietar/AFP/Getty Images Space US confirms for first time it has deployed weapons in space Analysts warn of an acceleration in high-risk arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit Oliver Holmes Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.55 EDT First published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US has deployed weapons in space, the US military has confirmed, in an extraordinary public announcement that analysts warn will accelerate a high-risk arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit. The US secretary of the air force, Troy Meink, said Washington had active “on-orbit” weapons, meaning they had been deployed and were circling the globe. “Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said on Monday at the annual Air, Space , Cyber conference. “This is why the United States now has, on-orbit, space-control weapons.” Meink said he would not go into the “specifics” of the weapons. However, a US Space Force spokesperson said space control could refer to “employing kinetic [combat] and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities”. The statement added that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”. Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”. In Moscow, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters that Russia believed “that space must be free of any weapon” and called for “the complete demilitarisation of space”. It has been an open secret that the US, Russia and China are working on space weapons, which could include signal jammers to disable other satellites or more “kinetic” options including those that fire projectiles. Still, space experts warn a public confirmation of such capabilities in orbit for the first time could accelerate a risky arms race. The astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who has spent decades compiling a list of rocket launches, told the Guardian it was reasonable to assume Washington had such weapons in space, probably jammers, as it had already deployed several satellites with secret payloads. He said that after the announcement, Russia and China would now “respond in kind” and deploy their own weapons. “In the long run, I find it questionable whether this is in the US national interest, and for sure we will see comparable systems from China, if they don’t already have them,” he said. ‘This feels fragile’: how a satellite-smashing chain reaction could spiral out of control Read more Even radio jamming would be a big escalation of military activity in space, said McDowell, who worked at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics until he retired this year. Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation’s chief director of space security and stability, told the Defence One website that the US now had to accept that the Chinese and Russians would do the same. “Well, that’s huge, because I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” she said. While the militarisation of space began in the 1950s with both Washington and Moscow exploring ways to destroy satellites, there have been attempts over the decades to preserve the emptiness around Earth for peaceful means. In 1967, superpowers and other countries signed the outer space treaty, which banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit, although the text does not contain a general prohibition on placing conventional weapons in Earth orbit. The end of the cold war in 1989 brought a moment of cooperation – including the in-orbit assembly of the International Space Station by multiple nations – but in the 21st century space has gradually become a potential battlefield. Russia sparked international criticism in 2021 when it struck one of its defunct satellites in orbit in a test of a ground-based anti-satellite missile. The blast created thousands of pieces of orbital debris. As satellites zip around the Earth at thousands of miles an hour, the fear is that an orbital confrontation will lead to a domino effect where the space near Earth becomes cluttered with tiny, high-speed bits of metal. McDowell said that in the US, the mentality of working towards the solely peaceful use of space was changing. “The US sees conflict in space as something that is conceptually normalised, whereas 20 years ago it was ‘no, we will never want to do that’,” he said. “I think this is wrong,” he added. “I also think it is still not too late to change course on this. To work mainly with China, because they are the real competitors in space now. I hope the US establishment takes a step back and rethinks some of this.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report Explore more on these topics Space US military Russia China Weapons technology news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story BAE agrees to buy space technology firm Ball Aerospace for $5.6bn UK ‘very interested’ in hosting US Space Force radar station Britain and US accuse Russia of launching 'weapon' in space Space wars: Trump's ready for his next big fight – in orbit Nato leader identifies space as the next ‘operational domain’ ‘It’s going to happen’: is the world ready for war in space? US News Russian Intelligence Operatives Charged by DOJ in Connection to Terrorism, Murder-for-Hire Plots The DOJ alleges that Russian Intelligence Services recruited a U.S. resident to monitor and murder a prominent Russian dissident in the United States. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Attorney General of the United States Todd Blanche speaks at Day 1 of the 2026 Republican National Committee (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026. John Fredricks/The Epoch Times Jill McLaughlin 9/15/2026 | Updated: 9/18/2026 0:00 X 1 Russians intelligence operatives believed to be part of a global assassination network operating in the United States were charged Sept. 15 in connection with murder-for-hire plots in the United States and with terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in Europe perceived to be aligned with Ukraine. The wanted suspects allegedly attempted to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the request of the Kremlin, according to Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg. The defendants remained at large Tuesday, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) said. “The charges announced today represent the culmination of extraordinary work by multiple FBI field offices, components, and partner agencies that collectively disrupted Russia’s attempts to conduct violent acts in our nation’s capital and throughout the United States,” Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI Washington Field Office Darren B. Cox said. Three of the defendants are high-ranking members of the Russian Intelligence Services. Yuri Khrameev, known as “Colonel Yuri,” 63, of Russia, is a former colonel in the services and has allegedly helped recruit several people to commit murder against perceived Russian dissidents, according to the DOJ. Related Stories Justice Department Counters Russian Military Intelligence Unit Attack on US Targets Russian Hackers Accessing WhatsApp, Signal Users’ Accounts, Say Dutch Intelligence Agencies Kirill Khrameev, 27, of Russia, is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia and Yuri Khrameev’s son. The third high-ranking member is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, a Cuban national and an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia. He has coordinated attacks for the Russian Intelligence Services, according to DOJ officials. Another defendant charged is Yodel Delgado Suarez, also known as “Viking,” 35, of Cuba, who is a prolific recruiter for the Russian Intelligence Services network. Suarez has allegedly recruited or tried to recruit multiple people in the United States. Defendant Eduardo Castro, 22, of Venezuela, is suspected of working with Suarez in the recruitment of U.S.-based assassins to surveil and try to murder a prominent U.S.-based Russian dissident. “It is our job to stop America’s adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. “And that’s precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors.” The Russian intelligence network has allegedly carried out or conspired to carry out multiple schemes around the world, according to the DOJ. Assistant Director Darren Cox Counterintelligence Division Special Agent attends a press conference about the White House Correspondents' Dinner shooting, at the Justice Department in Washington on April 27, 2026. Madalina Kilroy/The Epoch Times This summer, the network allegedly recruited a U.S. resident to monitor and murder a prominent Russian dissident they thought was living in the United States. Prosecutors say Suarez sent the hired resident to two locations to surveil the victim, gave his accomplice instruction about how to conduct the surveillance, and promised the resident between $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the surveillance. The resident allegedly returned several photos and videos to Suarez, according to the DOJ. Suarez and Castro are accused of offering the recruited resident another $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the victim, the DOJ said. They also allegedly indicated they had other targets within the United States. Kirill Khrameev is accused of recruiting a U.S. citizen to travel to a victim’s home to take photos for money. His father, Yuri Khrameev, offered the person $25,000 to kill the victim, according to prosecutors. Durruthy is accused of coordinating travel and logistics for the network, and for orchestrating terror attacks in Prague, Czechia, and in Lithuania. Both Khrameevs, Durruthy, Suarez, and Castro are charged with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. The elder Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro are also charged with participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. “We will stamp out any foreign intelligence services’ attempt to operate freely in our great Nation, and we will not rest until they and their enablers suffer the most severe consequences that federal law can levy,” Eisenberg said.
